title: Miketz: guilt remembers (Genesis 42:21)
hook: years later the brothers say "We are verily guilty concerning our brother"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hanukkah portion: Pharaoh's dreams and lights in the dark season. Your line was dreams in the dark. What light did you turn on? Today, the famine reaches Canaan. Day two hundred nine.

Something you did at fourteen. A cruel thing you said to a kid at school. You haven't thought about it in years. Then one day, something small, a song, a name, a face in a crowd, and it's right there again, as sharp as the day it happened. Famine has come, just as Joseph said. In Canaan, Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain. They stand before the governor of Egypt, and bow low. They don't recognize him. He recognizes them. Today: guilt remembers.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU DID AT FOURTEEN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, BOWING.` → `THEY DON'T RECOGNIZE HIM.`

segments.voice: Joseph speaks to them harshly, through an interpreter. You're spies. You've come to find the weak spots in our land. They protest: we're honest men, twelve brothers, sons of one father. The youngest is at home with our father, and one is no more. Joseph puts them in custody for three days. Then he tells them: one of you stays in prison, the rest take grain home, and bring me your youngest brother. And right there, in front of him, the brothers start talking to each other in Hebrew, thinking the Egyptian can't understand. And what comes out, more than twenty years after the pit, is this, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother." We saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. That's why this distress has come on us. Notice what they remember. Not just the act. His begging. The Torah never told us, back at the pit, that Joseph pleaded with them. We only learn it now, from their memory. Guilt kept a detail that the story itself left out. Reuben adds: didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy? And you wouldn't listen. And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away from them and weeps. The Hebrew phrase the brothers use, aval ashemim anachnu, is where their teshuvah, their turning back, begins. Its key word is ashem, guilty, which echoes in the confession Jews say on Yom Kippur: ashamnu, we have been guilty. Said together, out loud. Guilt remembers. And remembering is where repair begins.
screen: `YOU ARE SPIES.` · `ONE OF US IS NO MORE.` · `WE SAW HIS DISTRESS, AND WOULD NOT HEAR.` · `JOSEPH TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.` · then, large: `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a guilt you still carry. Settle, and breathe. Let one old thing come up, something you did, or didn't do, that still stings. Don't argue with it, and don't drown in it. Just name it, quietly, the way the brothers did: I did this. I saw, and didn't listen. If you pray, you can bring it to God. Then ask: is there anything, even small, I could do to repair it? The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion where, years later, the brothers finally say out loud, we are verily guilty concerning our brother.
Your line: guilt remembers. Today, if an old wrong comes to mind, don't push it away. Write it down, or take one small step toward making it right. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, Jews confess together in the plural, beginning ashamnu, we have been guilty, and Jewish teaching on teshuvah includes naming the wrong aloud and seeking to repair it.

fork.setup: you're one of the brothers. the governor of Egypt accuses you of spying and keeps one of you in prison. what goes through your mind?
options: this is because of what we did to our brother.
fork.reveal: they said, we are verily guilty concerning our brother: we saw his distress and would not hear.

original.note: Hebrew: truly, we are guilty. the brothers' words, more than twenty years after the pit.

trapdoor: what you thought: the brothers got caught.
what it means: long-buried guilt surfaces, and they finally name it aloud.
what a scholar hears: Joseph's begging in the pit appears only here, in the brothers' memory (Genesis 42:21), not in the scene itself (37:23–24).

sources.quoted: We are verily guilty concerning our brother

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 42:21 (the rest of the verse is paraphrased).
'More than twenty years after the pit' is inferred from Joseph's ages (17 at the sale, 30 before Pharaoh, plus seven years of plenty and the start of famine); confirm.
Linking aval ashemim anachnu to the Ashamnu confession is a thematic echo, not a claim of liturgical derivation; confirm framing.
'Journey of teshuvah' framing for the brothers is common in commentary; confirm.
Audit (second sample): replaced the stock phrase 'begins a long journey of teshuvah' with a plain line; no change to the facts.
